speechtext: I understand that in addition to this item we have to consider items 763, 727 and 541.

Last night I was making
some observations and asking some questions with respect to the construction of the head office building for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I had asked the minister to, give the cost of construction of a floor of the building, and I presume there will be no difficulty about that. The answer at page 820 of Hansard for December 17, 1952, indicates that the spring floor or the so-called "recreation floor" cost an additional $2,500. Could we have the cost of construction of the whole floor, please?
The cost of construction of the whole floor was $7,500.

I cannot imagine that is the cost of construction of a floor of the building. Surely the way to arrive at the cost of constructing the floor is to take the number of floors and divide the number into the total cost of constructing the building. Perhaps we had better start with the total cost of construction; could we have that figure please?
The total cost of construction of the building, Mr. Chairman, was $1,800,000.
Is that figure now complete?
Yes, sir.
I presume that is the building only, and does not include either land or equipment?
That is correct.
Or landscaping?
That is correct.

What is the total space?
Would the minister give it whichever way he prefers, either the floor space or the cubic feet of space in the building, and how much of that is assigned to this so-called recreation floor.
The cubic content of the building is 1,750,000 cubic feet.
And this floor?
The area of the floor is 6,000 square feet.

Last night the minister indicated that, on a cubic foot basis, the cost of erecting this building compared favourably with that of other buildings. Can he give us the figure as to the cubic foot cost of the construction of the building?
I am told that the cubic foot cost of the building is about $1.08.

What facilities does the building contain apart from space directly assigned to office use? Last night I asked about the auditorium. From the minister's answer I was not clear whether the auditorium is on a separate floor from the recreation floor or whether he was treating them together. Will the minister clarify that question with respect to the auditorium and its cost? I asked for some information about specifications and so on. Can he tell us something more about the auditorium? Then I presume there are cafeteria facilities. Perhaps the minister could say a word about that matter also, and any other facilities that could be classified as facilities designed to accommodate the employees, apart from office space.

The non-working space consists largely of a cafeteria and the auditorium which has been referred to in the house occasionally as the recreation area. It is one and the same thing. There are only the two, the cafeteria and the auditorium.
The answer to question No. 5 at page 820 of Hansard indicates that the auditorium cost $40,000.
That is correct. The figure I gave my hon. friend was just for the floor. The $7,500 was just for the floor.

Then we have been at cross purposes because when I was speaking about the floor I was thinking rather about the storey of the building, not just the covering that people walk on. That fact perhaps explains why this figure for the cost of the floor looked to me to be disproportionately small. Whether he works it out in actual figures or on the cubic foot calculation, can the minister tell us what was the cost of the
Supply-Resources and Development construction of that storey of the building known as the recreation floor?

I do not know how accurately I can get at those figures of the cost of construction of a particular room within a building. But as I indicated in a return tabled earlier, the cost of the auditorium was approximately $40,000. The floor area, as I said earlier, was 6,000 square feet. The height is about 22 feet. That means that there is a cubic content there of about 132,000 cubic feet at a total cost of $40,000.
Again those figures do not jibe. The minister indicated that the over-all cost of the construction of that building had worked out at $1.08 per cubic foot.
Yes.

If the cubic content of this
storey of the building is 132,000 cubic feet, then obviously the cost of the construction of that storey was something like $145,000.
A dollar a foot.

At $1.08 per cubic foot, if
the cubic foot content of that storey of the building is 132,000 cubic feet as the minister has indicated, I think he will agree that would indicate a cost of construction of that storey of approximately $145,000.

Mr. Chairman, as I said before, it is extremely difficult to allocate costs of a particular room within a building. There is nothing in this room. It is just an empty space of 132,000 cubic feet; and it is estimated that, as such, it cost $40,000. If my hon. friend wishes to take the $1.08 which is the average cost per cubic foot of the whole building, and allocate that same unit of cost to the 132,000 cubic feet, then he would arrive at the figure which he has just put before the committee. But on the basis of additional cost for this 132,000 cubic feet as such, it is estimated that it was $40,000.
May I ask a question with reference to the auditorium? I gather that there are no stationary seats in it. It is open; it has been left open?
Yes.
Is there any stage?

There is a small platform.
There are no fixed seats in the auditorium.

What persons are entitled
to use the auditorium? I presume we can refer to the recreation floor and the auditorium as being synonymous?

One and the same thing.

Supply-Resources and Development
May I ask what persons are entitled to make use of that floor, at what times, and for what purposes?

The purpose of the auditorium was to provide, in the first place, a room large enough to accommodate the employees of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, for meeting purposes, particularly when the field people are brought in- so they can meet together. Hitherto they have had no place where that could be done. It also provides an area sufficiently large to enable the corporation to exhibit the vast number of drawings it has occasionally for display purposes and for models of small houses. I see that the hon. member for Lake Centre does not believe that.
I was wondering whether a spring floor was necessary for that.
I was wondering that same thing.
He is greatly surprised, that is all, knowing the minister as he does. He could not stand it.
However, I will continue to deal with facts and let my hon. friends draw their own conclusions.
Do they separate them out on the floor?
It also provides space to develop and display models of small houses. My hon. friends may not know it, but that is quite an operation.
A child with its blocks.

At the same time it provides a recreational area where, some two nights a week, the employees of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are permitted to play badminton. The area, of course, can also be used as a dance floor. I am told that in the approximately one year the building has been in use up to date it has been used for dance purposes about four times.

About 600.
How many employees of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are there in the building?

It is built for capacity attendance?
It is built for 600 people.

The minister has indicated that there have been four dances there since


the building was opened. When was the building opened?
Then I note that the building is open two nights a week for badminton. What happens on the other nights of the week?
The room is in darkness.

Who are entitled to make
use of this recreation floor for badminton or for dances?

The employees of Central
Mortgage and Housing Corporation.

Before the building was
constructed with these facilities included, was the government consulted about it, and did it [DOT] give its approval to the construction of these additional facilities?
Yes.

I thank the minister for his answers. He has given straight answers to straight questions, and I thank him for his frankness. At this stage of the session, Mr. Chairman, I shall not say as much as I think the occasion calls for, but I will say this. While we all recognize the importance of the work assigned to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation-and it is a very heavy responsibility that has been assigned to that corporation, and we wish to see adequate accommodation provided for the operating and administrative needs of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation-nevertheless what has been said here today and last night on this subject simply does not justify expenditure of money of the taxpayers of Canada on this floor in the way that has been indicated.
A spring floor for dances and badminton may be very valuable. There are many people in this country who would like to have facilities of that kind available to them, but they have to get along without them or provide them as best they can out of fees they contribute to organizations or associations, to enjoy those advantages.
I have always said I would like to see the government a model employer, but I think this is going beyond reason. The suggestion was offered last night that because this building is located some distance from downtown Ottawa it justified the inclusion in this building of a whole floor for recreational purposes, so called.
It is not an entire floor.

The fact is that the distance that most of those who are employed in it are from there is all the more reason to

indicate there was no necessity for including this expensive facility in this building, because those who make use of it in the two nights a week that it is open for badminton obviously come some distance to be there.
We are told there have been four dances there since it was opened last July. That is a period of ten months.

Do they supply special
buses to get them there?

I think it is going to be
a fair question to put to every taxpayer in this country:	Are you satisfied to have your
money used under these circumstances to provide in this handsome structure a whole floor.
Six thousand square feet.
Six thousand square feet.
On one floor.

Six thousand square feet to be set aside for the use that has been indicated by the minister. The use that has been indicated thus far by the minister to have made of these facilities in a period of ten months is two nights a week for badminton and a total of four dances.
Money does not come to the taxpayers of this country as easily as that. The easy course that money takes is when the government gets hold of it. They spend it too easily; they spend it without a sense of responsibility.
The last condemnation of this matter is the fact that the government approved of that expenditure before it was made; because the minister has frankly indicated that the government did approve the inclusion of these facilities in this building before the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation went ahead with it at a cost of $1,800,000. It is one more evidence of the fact that in matters of money, as well as in many other ways that we see daily here, this government has lost all sense of responsibility to this house and to the taxpayers of Canada.

I do not think any hon. member could listen to the argument that was put up by the hon. member without recalling to him some of the things that have happened before, things that have been well planned and turned out to the advantage of all the people of the country. I should like to recall to him that at the time Sir John A. Supply-Resources and Development as the hon. member for Eglinton has just used in regard to our minister that this was planning for a thousand years ahead, and would never be used. You and I have lived to see the day when these buildings are not big enough.

You look it up in the library.

When these buildings were
planned by Sir John A. Macdonald there was a Liberal premier, if you wish, who said that at that time they looked to be much too large and far too pretentious. It is all very well for a lawyer to rise in his place and mislead the public with a great flow of eloquent language and with no regard for engineering principles whatever. It is all very well for him to try to mislead the people into thinking that mistakes have been made. And cost $2,500.

And have office employees
bouncing along the whole floor in years to come, tiptoeing through the twilight. They talk about 'looking to the future. They will have a night staff; they will have clever government employees in the future. They will not be similar to anything we have today. My hon. friend's statement indicates that we shall have no dances over there in the future. All the government employees will be ballet dancers. We are going to lose all that in the future because the floor space with the springs is going to be used for ordinary clerical work. At that time we are going to dispense with the dance floor, and after all the government employees have learned how to dance. That is one of the best stories I have ever heard.
I have a great deal of respect for my hon. friend and also for the minister. I ask:	If
either of these gentlemen were in private business, drawing up plans for a building, which plans would have to be passed by the stockholders or members of the association, would he include plans for dance floors, badminton floors, cafeterias and restaurants? When it is their money they can do what they like with it; but not when it is not their money. Recently I read about an oil man in Texas worth $100 million. He had five or six houses and 30 Cadillacs, all bought with his own money. The facts were written up in Collier's magazine, to show just what a fool a man could be with money.
But this is not the minister's money. This money does not belong to the hon. member for Wellington South; this is the taxpayers' money. Let the taxpayer decide what recreation the civil servants should have. Surely the 600 employees in the civil service who work in that building do not live within a quarter of a mile of it. The fact is that the building is away out on the Montreal road, and it would be a great inconvenience for them to go there for their recreation. It would be most inconvenient to go out there to play badminton at night.


How many employees in any first-class private corporation in Canada have dance halls and badminton courts? No, they want to get away from the buildings in which they work. I am sure that on second thought the minister will never repeat this procedure of putting a dance floor in other buildings he has anything to do with. He has referred to the cost as being only $2,500. But let me say to him that that means $10 each for 250 burnt-out pensioners who need that $10. The pen should be used in connection with these expenditures; it should be used on every five-cent piece.
When Mr. King was prime minister a five-cent piece put him out of office. It was not $2,500. We are all here as representatives of the taxpayers. I believe the members of the government and their supporters regret exceedingly that this government has now approved this example of introducing dance floor and badminton courts into business offices connected with the federal government. And if other ministers recommend the installation of this costly equipment in every new building across Canada, it will run into millions of dollars, not $2,500. You cannot make flesh of one and fowl of another. The whole thing is ridiculous and I am sorry to see the minister doing it.
Oh, oh.
Oh, you can laugh. That is your privilege. You should be ashamed to laugh at a matter like this.
That is silly.
You are just laughing; all you do is laugh. Get up on your feet and say something.

Mr. Chairman, I do not purpose saying very much about this item. However, the discussion does indicate a very healthy condition of affairs when estimates presented running into millions of dollars receive the attention this one has received. Indeed, one of the major criticisms of parliament is that estimates are brought down during the dying days of a session with the result that, usually, only a farcical examination is made of them.
This item has been dealt with, and dealt with thoroughly. I think that what has happened in the last couple of days is further evidence of the necessity for a reorganization of parliament to bring it into keeping with present-day conditions. If the estimates were made available to a committee, as are the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, they would receive proper examination, and parliament would discharge its responsibility.

But inevitably the rush for prorogation leads to a lack of examination. That is one of the first things the new parliament will have to face. For certainly, as the situation is today, any minister of the crown could place an estimate for $5 million in the estimates and cover it up with a little camouflage, and, regardless of whether there was any justification for it or not, it would pass, under normal circumstances.
It is not that easy to get items into the estimates.

No, perhaps it is not that easy to get them in the estimates. But I am not dealing with that. What I am dealing with is the fact that, if parliament is to maintain its dignity and importance, we must alter our rules so as to provide for the examination of these estimates during the session. While generally I am an opponent of the committee system, I do believe that if committees in respect of the various departments were set up similar to the one dealing with the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, there would be a much more careful and complete examination of expenditures.
Having said that, I join with the hon. member for Eglinton in his reference to the expenditure revealed in the item before the committee. The minister, with commendable frankness, to which tribute has already been paid by reason of its being unusually unique, has told the committee that the government approved of the expenditure in advance.
The people of Canada do not want their money spent in this way. However, the other day, during the course of the discussion on his estimates in the house, another minister of the crown, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, when it was pointed out to him by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra that unjustifiable expenditures were being made in his department, made a comment which I believe will become almost immortal, when he said, "If the services say they need a gold-plated piano, it is our duty to buy it."
The example before the committee now is just another example of the gold-plated-piano type of mind:	Easy come, easy go.
That attitude of mind used to be restricted to one or two ministers; but apparently the spendthrift attitude has spread until today it covers all departments of government.
This is a very serious matter, to see money wasted in this way. For, after all, this body was set up to provide houses for Canadian people, not palaces for itself.
Supply-Resources and Development

I would like to take issue with the minister on the statement that this room cost only an additional $40,000. The minister, who is an engineer, must know-and I have very good reason to know, because I have participated in the building of a number of factory buildings and, quite recently, a community centre of which I am a director, and concerning which we gave careful consideration to the cost of additions and subtractions, discussing the matter with one of the most reputable builders in the country- that when you are considering the cost of any additional room in a building you take the average cost per cubic foot, and multiply it by the number of cubic feet which will be added in view of the addition of that room. And that is the cost of the room.
The extra cost of this dance floor is not $40,000; it is simply $1.08 per cubic foot multiplied by 132,000 cubic feet, or approximately $145,000. I think that ought to be put clearly on the record; because the minister and his department know perfectly well that that is the way costs are figured. I wanted to have that straight.

Obviously the hon. member
who has just taken his seat is not a contractor. He is totally unhampered by knowledge of building costs, and has offered figures that any contractor would laugh at.
I am not at all surprised that there has been considerable criticism of this item. In every community there will be found a group of conservative-thinking people who will oppose school boards when they suggest the building of an auditorium in a new school. These folk have a right to their own opinion, but fortunately they are not the majority. Wherever you go across Canada you will find new public buildings. In most of our rural sections you will find new union schools which all have beautiful auditoriums. I suggest that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was reasonably modest in providing an auditorium 60 by 100, or whatever the dimensions are totalling 6,000 square feet. Surely in a country as wealthy as Canada the people who work for us are entitled to the normal amenities of life. Local school boards believe that they are spending the ratepayers' money wisely in building such auditoriums. I think now of one recently built in Nelson township adjoining my own town of Burlington. An auditorium almost the size of this auditorium under discussion is incorporated in a 12-room school. There was criticism of that.
May I ask my hon. friend a question?

All right.
5358	HOUSE OF
Supply-Resources and Development
Is the auditorium in the school in Nelson township, for example, made available for the use of the public or only employees of the township?
I do not style school students employees. I say that to the hon. member for Eglinton.
That is the difference.

The auditorium was built to extend additional amenities of life to the school children. Surely Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation would not have been forward-looking and would not have been giving the same consideration to the welfare and well-being of its employees that it has shown in a business way in managing this highly profitable institution if it had not provided an auditorium. Is an auditorium 60 by 100 of an unreasonable size considering the tremendous size of the staff of the organization? These people are young people. Many of them are ex-servicemen and they want to have their badminton, their dances and so on. I am not surprised of course that conservative-thinking folk would be opposed to an expenditure of this kind, just as the same type of conservative-thinking folk in the township of Nelson did not want the school children to have an auditorium.

I am rather surprised to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Halton. It is a pretty clear indication that this gold-plated mentality is catching and has now extended from the cabinet down into the private members on the government side of the house. The hon. member has tried to compare a school auditorium with an office auditorium.
The same type of opposition, the same folk opposing.
I do not know whether he thinks that civil servants are all school children and should be treated as such, but that is the only inference that one can draw from his remarks.
The only inference that school children can draw from them.

There is absolutely no comparison between an auditorium for school children and an auditorium for the grown people working in this building. Unfortunately the attitude of the government in adopting such a policy is very unfair to a large group of people in Canada. There are still thousands of veterans who are living in basement one-room suites or living with relatives. They are living under terrible conditions all over the country. I know that there are many hundreds of them in that


position in the city of Vancouver. Here we have a corporation whose main job is to help provide housing for veterans and civilians who cannot get homes. The main obstacle to providing homes is the tremendous cost of construction today. This is one government body which should be showing how to build houses and other buildings cheaply. It should be showing how to save money, how to cut down the cost of a home.
The heads of the corporation and the minister responsible, instead of spending their energies trying to reduce costs for the benefit of those Canadians who are living under intolerable conditions, have authorized an expenditure in the headquarters of the corporation of at least $40,000, as the minister has admitted-
It is not a matter of admission; it was a statement.

Well, it is a statement and the minister is proud of it. They have authorized the expenditure of $40,000 to instal an auditorium, including a dance floor, in the headquarters of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. What worries me about the whole thing is the thinking of the minister and the senior men in the corporation, and the fact that they would even consider taking a step of this kind. It shows how far removed they are from the needs of the people of the country. It shows how little possibility there is of their ever settling the housing problem. I cannot understand how the minister could take the attitude he has taken on this question.
There is need for government help in great developments such as our atomic energy program. Yet the scientists working on that program are doing their work in the basement of the museum while Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation goes out on the Montreal road and builds a $2 million office building with a $40,000 auditorium. This action is unfair to every other department of government. It is unfair to every city and town of Canada that a lead of this kind should be given by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I hope that this bad example will not be carried any further and that some steps will be taken by the minister to see that from now on the heads of this corporation-I am not criticizing the employees but the direction-will concentrate their energies on the real problem facing them, the finding of houses for Canadian people who do not have a home at the present time.

I think perhaps I should try to bring this matter back into proper perspective after some of the irrelevant speeches that have just been made by some members of the opposition. I must say that I think

the hon. member for Eglinton has tried to keep the matter in perspective, and I welcome criticism when it is made in that light. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has just said that this is a bad example. I wonder whether or not government employees all across Canada will think that it is a bad example on the part of the government and the taxpayers of Canada to try to provide working conditions which are comparable-and the hon. member for Eglinton said this morning that they should be comparable-with conditions provided by good employers throughout the country. I know of no large office building in this country, and I doubt whether the hon. member for Broadview with all his experience as a director knows of any, that is not equipped with a suitable auditorium. On the other hand, I do know of companies that have had to undertake the great expense of constructing auditoriums in their buildings after they had been completed. There is a very real need for sufficient space in any large building to enable the staff to get together for conferences. I doubt whether any member of the opposition will deny that that is part of good administration in any organization. If there is, I would be glad to have him say so-to say whether or not this is a bad example.

May I ask the minister a
question at that point? How many times has the entire staff been assembled in that auditorium for business conferences?
There you have it.
Quite as often as employees of insurance companies.
I have not seen them.
Get around the country and you will see some of them.
Get around your own backyard and you do not see anything like that.
I do not have the record or the diary of the corporation and I do not know the number of times that the auditorium has been used.
You don't have any record so there has been no use.

There have been meetings
in the auditorium on many occasions. Recently civil defence used the auditorium and found it a very good place.

Perhaps
they could have found other places as convenient.

Perhaps they could, but I say that here is space that can be used and is used to advantage by the people of Central
Supply-Resources and Development Mortgage and Housing. It is available for others in the interests of the general public. Now, this space was provided as an auditorium. Does any member of the opposition say that there should not be an auditorium in this building?
Yes.

The suggestion has been
made that the objective of Central Mortgage and Housing should be to encourage the building of houses in this country. With that I agree. If I did not agree I would not be devoting to the problem the time I am devoting to it. The hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra said this was an example of extravagance. I ask him if he thinks that a building of this size, produced at a cost of $1.08 per cubic foot, is an example of extravagance. Can he tell me that he can point to any other similar building that can be produced for that cost? I think that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, by selecting land which was relatively low cost land in this high cost area, and building that type of building where space utilization is high and where the cost per cubic foot is low, has set an example that might well be followed by people building large scale office accommodation across this country, whether these offices be for public use or for private use.
The question seems to resolve itself in the minds of the opposition as to whether there should be an auditorium and whether $40,000 is too much money to spend for that additional accommodation. I can see the argument which the hon. member for Broadview will advance and it is the type of argument that one must consider; but I simply state that this accommodation was provided at a cost of $40,000-and that is a correct statement of the facts. I leave it to the taxpayers of this country, to the voters of this country, and I am prepared even to leave it to the good judgment of some members of the opposition-
The spring floor as well?

-to say whether or not there should be an auditorium in a building which houses 632 employees under the circumstances in which those people are employed. If it is conceded that there should be an auditorium-
That was never conceded.
I concede it. I think the public servants of Canada will concede it and I think the taxpayers will concede it.

Hear, hear.

Supply-Resources and Development
May I ask the minister, if he approves of it for this building, whether he approves of constructing an auditorium in the same type of buildings belonging to the federal government across Canada?
Under the circumstances, yes.
For every building with the same number of employees do you suggest that we should now construct an auditorium and a dance floor? Do you approve of that?
This government considers every problem on its merits.
Come, come.

Under similar conditions my answer is yes. I say that there should be an auditorium and, if there is doubt in anyone's mind about its design, I will say that we called on the advice of the best architects we could find. The architects who prepared the plans and designed the building included in their recommendations the suggestion that this floor should be built. As I told hon. members, it was built. We asked the architects if it was common practice to build floors of this kind and they said that in accordance with modern architectural and construction practice it was desirable. That was their recommendation. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation accepted the recommendation and, Mr. Chairman, I am prepared to stand by it. I am prepared to leave it to the taxpayers of this country and to the good judgment of citizens of Canada generally as to whether this building is the sort of building that is a credit to the people of Canada. Moreover, I am willing to leave it to the same judges as to whether or not Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is doing a good job in the interests of the citizens of Canada.

The minister has now come to the defence of this proposition and naturally he would be expected to do so because he is the minister responsible for the department. Previously other supporters of the government have attempted to do so, and the hon. member for Halton especially made comparisons with school buildings. I do not think that on second reflection he would be able to justify the comparisons he made.
I would rather that you compare this with insurance company buildings.

He has used a comparison with school buildings. Well, naturally, when a school is built, because they have a large population in the school, they have to have an auditorium. They have almost daily congregation in the auditorium and it is an essential part of the school.
We always get the same type of opposition that we are getting today.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I intervene and say that when we reached these items last evening the house was co-operating towards concluding a study of the estimates of this department. Questions were put, answers were given and it was requested that these items stand until today.
I know that the general discussion which took place was very short and perhaps it was not taken advantage of as it should have been. Therefore, I did not want to curtail the discussion that has been taking place on this matter during the last hour. However, in case the situation that I have foreseen develops differently, perhaps I should say that nowhere in these four items is there any money to be spent towards the building we are discussing. Item 408 has to do with expenses incurred by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in constructing and supervising construction of married quarters, schools and related services on behalf of the Department of National Defence. Item 727 provides for the restoration of the special account in the consolidated revenue fund established by section 35 of the National Housing Act. Item 541 provides for advances to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the purposes of subsection 1 of section 34 of the National Housing Act in respect of housing projects for veterans and housing projects at Gander, Newfoundland. Item 763 has to do with section 35 of the National Housing Act.
As I say, discussion has carried on but I would hope that hon. members would perhaps come back to the co-operative spirit with which they were imbued last evening.
The hon. member for St. John's West may continue.
I would not have spoken if this controversy had not arisen.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Before proceeding, Mr. Chairman, I wonder if you would inform the committee just which one of these items we are on. I want to be sure that I do not miss the item having to do with section 35.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I know that the hon. member is interested in item 727 and in order to provide the widest possible latitude I have kept the four items before me-because the minute I say we are discussing item 408, then, definitely, the hon. member is more out of order than ever. As I say, if hon. members wish to discuss this matter of the building all day, I shall be sorry that I ever tolerated the discussion in the first place. If the hon. member is the last speaker on this subject,

perhaps we can revert to item 408 and then have our remarks relevant to the item.

I would not have entered into this controversy if you had not tolerated it so far, Mr. Chairman, but I could not resist answering the argument made by the hon member for Halton, which seems to be so irrelevant and illogical. This is the case of a government building, and the minister had stated it correctly. He stands by it. He says this is a government building, and we wish to behave like private employers. But you are not dealing with private money, you are dealing with public money. I say that neither this minister nor any other minister is the person who should provide amenities of that kind. Necessities should be provided, yes, but not facilities for entertainment like that. If you do that you will be establishing a principle which the government will have to follow all over Canada, to provide similar amenities in all the other buildings.
The minister speaks of a building with 632 employees. Is he going to limit it to a building containing that number of people? What about a building containing 500 or 400 or 300? Where are you going to draw the line? Are they not equally entitled to have a dance floor and badminton courts? If this criticism had not arisen, would the minister go on to provide tennis courts and football fields for those who like outdoor amusements, as well as those who like indoor amusements? I do not think this is justified. When the minister speaks about the general public, has the general public been invited or actually used this building? There are many other auditoriums in this city that could be used for this purpose without going to the considerable expense of erecting this building. I think this is a policy that should stop right here, unless we want to go completely into a socialistic policy, and that is a tendency that this Liberal government has shown for many years.
You were kind enough to suggest, Mr. Chairman, that perhaps the committee should come within the provisions of the section, and I now wish to do that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Of item 408?

Yes. I want to ask the
minister a number of questions concerning this item, which is for the provision of the expenses incurred by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in constructing and supervising construction of married quarters, schools and related services on behalf of the Department of National Defence. The amount asked for is $700,000. I return to a subject that comes four-square within the purview of this section, namely construction contracts for the Booth Construction Company Limited
Supply-Resources and Development at Camp Borden. The questions which I asked in relation to this matter were passed as an order for return on May 9. The answer which I have received indicates that this company has been engaged during the past four years by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to do certain construction work at Camp Borden, the amount of the contract being $2,148,336. These contracts cover four different types of construction and public works totalling some 394 housing units as well as the sewers and water mains.
This company did not complete these contracts, and in particular the construction of 100 housing units under one contract and 90 under another. One question which I asked was as follows:
Were the subcontractors of the said company, or suppliers of goods, wares or merchandise or services, in connection with the said contract or contracts duly paid?
The answer was that, although the contracts are with the prime contractor, the Booth Construction Company Limited only, the prime contractor and some of the contractors and suppliers have informed Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation that there remain outstanding amounts to some subcontractors and suppliers of materials.
Then, the last question was:
If not, what is the total amount of the unpaid indebtedness of the said company to each of the subcontractors or suppliers, giving the amounts owing and the names and addresses of each of them.
Now, when this matter came up the other day I pointed out that I would, on Monday, make an application to the house. Unfortunately, under the rules such a matter can only be brought up under circumstances that would require almost a week's notice. The suggested course that I had in mind was not followed, and is not being followed because of the fact that, generally speaking, the house desires to have its proceedings come to an end. Therefore, I follow the course of asking a few questions of the minister.
To my question as to what was the unpaid indebtedness, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation stated they received representations from Booth Construction Company Limited, suppliers and subcontractors, but the representations are insufficient to provide an answer to this question, both as to the list of creditors and the amount owing on account of these two jobs. Now then, Mr. Chairman, accepting that answer in its form, I shall amend the question so as to permit of the information being given. The amended question will be, what is the total amount of the unpaid indebtedness of the said company of which the department or the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has had notice?

Supply-Resources and Development Then, I would ask the minister to let the committee know how many contractors have communicated with the department or with the corporation complaining that they were not paid. Thirdly, I should like the minister to place before the committee, in summary form, the provisions of the contract with the Booth Construction Company Limited which deal with the necessity of the contractor supplying proof that the subcontractors have, indeed, been paid before advances are made. I ask him, too, whether or not this company produced affidavits or statutory declarations setting out that the subcontractors were paid. When I have those answers, I then have one or two other questions.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I could make a few general remarks, and then the hon. member for Lake Centre might wish me to give particulars beyond that. On June 1, 1950, a contract for the construction of 100 houses at Camp Borden was awarded to R. F. Booth Construction Limited, and on June 9 a further contract for 90 housing units was awarded to the same company. These contracts were let on a firm price basis.
In each case a security deposit of $250 per house was taken by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation from the contractor. This amounted to $25,000 for the 100-house contract and $22,500 for the 90-house contract.
They were let on what basis? I did not catch that. The minister lowered his voice.

On a firm price basis. It was provided in the contract that progress payments should be made monthly to the contractor and that from such payments there would be retained a holdback of 10 per cent until the aggregate holdbacks reached $250 per unit. The contractor was required to furnish to Central Mortgage receipts from all subcontractors and suppliers of materials indicating that such subcontractors and suppliers of materials had been paid up to the last previous advance.
In practice a contractor is obliged on making his second and all subsequent progress claims to submit a statement, verified by statutory declaration, to the effect that his accounts with subcontractors and suppliers of materials have been paid. In addition, he attaches the receipts I have mentioned.
Progress payments were made to R. F. Booth Construction Limited from July, 1950, to September, 1951, according to the procedure that I have outlined. In September, 1951, the Booth Construction company was experiencing financial difficulties, and on

September 28 the corporation was obliged to make special arrangements so that the contracting company would meet its payroll account. From this time on until December 5, 1951, the contractor was endeavouring to arrange his affairs so that he might complete his contract, and during that time the corporation made interim advances for the purpose of meeting further payroll accounts.
How much were they?
I will have that information later.
That is all right.

On December 5, 1951, the contractor was obliged to discontinue operations on both contracts and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation took over the projects to make arrangements for the completion of construction.
At the time of the take-over of the contracts by the corporation there was about $105,000 remaining in the contract accounts. In addition, the corporation held the security deposits and the holdbacks. These totalled approximately $95,000. The cost to complete the contract was in excess of the total amount remaining in the contracts, plus security deposits and holdbacks. The overrun amounted to approximately $21,000.
R. F. Booth Construction Limited, the contractor, and Booth Equipment and Supply Company Limited, an allied firm, took advan-take of the Companies Creditors Arrangement Act, with a view to getting their affairs in order.
In March, 1952, Central Mortgage received a copy of an auditor's report as at January 31, 1952, relating to the two companies. This report sets forth a list of creditors of the construction company under the following headings:
Accounts payable-trade	(unsecured),
total	 $73,787.95
Creditors preferred as to special banking
arrangements	 8,582.60
Total trade accounts	 $82,370.55
Accounts payable-subcontractors (unsecured)	 $36,716.13
Creditors preferred as to special banking
arrangements	 6,658.45
Total subcontractors	 $43,374.58
There is no indication in these statements as to whether the trade accounts or the subcontractors' accounts relate to the contracts with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, nor is there any indication as to what has happened to these accounts since January, 1952.

Shall the item
carry?

Will the minister now answer the particular questions that I asked? Will he read into the record that portion of the contract that deals with progress reports and the need of supplying the statutory declaration setting out that the amounts in fact have been paid?
I have not a copy of the actual contract with me.

Surely the officers have a copy of the ordinary contract that is used, because the contracts are all the same with the exception of the fact that the names of the contractors will be different. Have the minister's officials none of those contracts or no duplicate forms?

If the minister will produce it after the lunch hour and let the committee have it, that will be satisfactory. These houses have all been completed since that time, have they?
Yes, sir.
Has the Booth Construction company been receiving any other contracts since 1951?
Not from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I am speaking about Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Then in so far as Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is concerned, the total amount of loss was $21,000?
That is right.

Were there available on the premises considerable quantities of plumbing equipment and other building equipment that was taken over by the contracting firm which took the place of Booth Construction company?

Mr. Chairman, I understand that when the difficulty became apparent,

Possibly we had better clarify that matter. Is it not a fact that the suppliers who had supplies there on consignment removed them but that those who had supplies there that were not on consignment were denied the right to remove them?

What was the value of the goods, wares, merchandise, plumbing equipment and the like on the premises that had not yet been used in any way at the time that Booth Construction company ceased operations? I now come to the next question. In view of the fact that in this case, as in others, innocent suppliers of goods, merchandise and services to government contractors have, in the last three or four years, been suffering losses, has any change been made or has any change been suggested in the form of contract in order to protect these individuals who have no right to file mechanics' liens or to take other measures to protect themselves, except, of course, the right to take action? What is being done to seal up this apparent unfairness that permits of grave injustices? That is a tremendous amount of money for subcontractors to lose. Even in the face of that material being

Mr. Chairman, I have only a very few remarks that I intend to make at this time in reference to the Department of Justice. I think, however, that one who was a member of the committee, if for only a matter of a few days when I found it impossible to my great regret to continue on that committee, it would not be amiss if I were to express personally and also on behalf

of the opposition commendation to that committee on amendments to the Criminal Code. It was an outstanding committee. It was an example of the way in which a committee should operate. The committee was composed of men who were well able to discuss the subject under consideration and I think it will remain a model for a very long time to come of the means and methods whereby committees may operate for the benefit of the country and for the preservation of the rule of law.
It is a matter of regret that at this session it has been impossible to deal with the recommendations made by that committee, but the voluminous nature of the bill and the many controversial questions which it would have been necessary to discuss had the bill been brought before the house, demanded that it be set over to the next parliament. I am sure that the work that was done by the committee will be made available to any committee set up in the next parliament. It will be of great assistance and will go a long way toward reducing the time required for further consideration in the committee.
There are some phases of criminal law that cannot be satisfactorily dealt with by that committee in the short time at its disposal. There are many phases of criminal law that are outdated and that will require a job to be done by either parliament or a committee recommending amendments that will have to be made to the Criminal Code in order to bring it up to the present advances in psychology and also to the general philosophy of law and of life itself. However, I do want to say a word for the committee and, at the same time, to say to the minister that his assistance in the committee and the contribution that he made to the commitee were worthy of the high traditions of the office which he occupies.
Having said that, there are one or two matters that I wish to deal with particularly, reserving of course the right to discuss some of the items when they come before the committee. I think one matter deserves special consideration and that is the question of combines investigation. It is a subject that in ever-increasing measure finds itself before parliament, and I think the time has come for a committee similar to the one on criminal law to be set up in order to canvass the whole concept regarding combines.
There are two different viewpoints. There is the American viewpoint which generally is founded on the premise that bigness is of itself inherently bad. There is the British concept that bigness of itself is not necessarily bad and that primarily what has to be considered is not the size of corporations, in the
Supply-Justice
modern world of large corporations, but whether or not the actions they take and their conduct are detrimental to public welfare. Our combines act is a product of judicial decisions, changes made by parliament in a rather haphazard manner, and other changes that are based on the experience of those who administer the act.
It is quite easy to pass legislation, but sometimes it is difficult to carry it into effect.
I have in mind particularly the debates that took place, Mr. Chairman, in December of 1951 when the question of price fixing was before the house. Resale price maintenance was a dangerous course of action, according to the minister, and the government legislation was passed.
At that time, we pointed out that the legislation would be ineffectual unless something was done in order to prevent the practice of loss leaders. I think the events of the last year have proven the correctness of our viewpoint. I understand that the officers in charge of the administration of the combines act have devoted themselves to an endeavour to secure a definition for "loss leader". I think the search has been a lost cause. In order to establish such a definition, as everyone knows, it must cover every possibility within the realm of comprehension, and as such is impossible of attainment.
One of the most interesting things in connection with price fixing was that recently the queen's printer, in the annual catalogue that was issued, stated that the prices that were fixed by the queen's printer were subject to a discount of 25 per cent to those who maintained the price set and fixed by the queen's printer as the resale price. This was an interesting sidelight. One department of government was making it an offence to fix the retail price at which a commodity is to be sold, and another department of government, the queen's printer, by public declaration was averring the need for this power to fix such prices in anticipation and also denying to those who fail to sell at the price fixed the right to secure the reduction or discount.
