The Criminal Code liability, then.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no limit.
The Criminal Code liability is what?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no limit at all. I think where my hon. friend has gone wrong is that he is thinking of the fine that was discussed the other day in Toronto in the cases there.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I refer to the recent rubber cases, in Toronto. But I am sure my hon. friend, as one who is familiar with the criminal law, is aware of the principle that where the law has been amended taking away the ceiling that formerly existed and making the penalty without limit at all, an offence which was committed when the law imposed a ceiling-
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -can only be punished by the law as it stood at the time when the offence was committed-
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -notwithstanding the fact that the prosecution may have been launched after the statute was amended.
I was coming to that. I know what my hon. friend is saying. He is saying that 'Vhen the offence took place, the penalty was $10,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I wanted to correct my hon. friend. My hon. friend made the bald and categorical statement that there was a ceiling of $10,000 upon these penalties.

Yes.

Supply-Justice

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is not quite correct. There is no ceiling whatsoever at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend says that I made a bald statement. If I did so, it was incorrect. What I am coming to is this. As to. the case in the city of Toronto where there had been wrongdoing over a period of time, a maximum penalty of $10,000 was not in keeping with the offence that was committed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I entirely agree.
That is the point I was making.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is the reason we amended the act.
I am coming to that matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend was here when we amended the act.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And he should be familiar with the amendment.

I am coming to that. There is no question about that. I am not going to argue with my hon. friend over that point. The penalty was totally out of keeping with the offence committed. Indeed, if my recollection is correct, some of the offences that were committed continued beyond the time or after the time of the amendment. My hon. friend may look that point up and find that I am correct in that regard, namely that some of the offences continued following the period in which the change in the law was made. Personally, I feel that, if the Combines Investigation Act is to be made effective, penalties in keeping with the crime will have to be brought into effect; that is, penalties that will penalize seriously enough to interfere with the gains that can be secured to directors who connive and contribute. Penalties are provided today. These penalties should consist of mandatory sentences of imprisonment; for where there is wrongdoing, such as has been revealed in some recent cases, it should be punished to the extreme limit. After all,^ the position of the state must be not to interfere with proper and fair competition but to make sure that there is free and uncontrolled competition. Otherwise, private enterprise cannot survive. There is only one way in which free enterprise operates and that is through equality of opportunity for the producer or the consumer. In effect, that is the essence of the combines legislation.

When wrongdoing is established, then amendments must be made to ensure that those who actively, or passively, if you like, act as directors shall not escape unscathed from a prison sentence. A fine is a poor substitute as a punishment for wrongdoing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: May I ask a question? A poor substitute for what?
A substitute for serious wrongdoing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend says that a fine is a poor substitute for a punishment.
For straight imprisonment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Can you imprison a corporation?

I am not talking about imprisoning a corporation; I am talking about the directors. It should be mandatory where a director acquiesces, either directly, or passively, by standing by, knowing that wrongdoing is taking place. The possibility of a fine being imposed is no deterrent to wrongdoing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I wonder whether I might reply to one or two points while they are fresh in the minds of the committee members. To begin with, I want to express my appreciation of and gratification at the complimentary remarks which the hon. member made concerning the special committee that considered Bill No. 93, respecting the criminal law. I think I can do that without immodesty, because although I was a member of the committee I really attended in my capacity of minister as an assistant, as it were, rather than as a member of the committee itself.
Everything the hon. member for Lake Centre has said about the committee is a compliment very well deserved by its members. During a period of some eight years I had the experience of being a member of a government which was set up for the express purpose of being non-partisan, and during five or six years I was the head of that government, so that I have some experience in working with members of other parties. But I can truthfully say that in all my public experience I never worked with a group of men on any committee or in any parliamentary connection who addressed themselves to the problem in hand with a greater lack of partisanship or a greater objectivity and a greater diligence than the members of the Criminal Code committee.
We had before us a measure which had been originally compiled by a very competent

royal commission, many of the members of which were amongst the most eminent criminal lawyers in Canada. Its product went to the other place. A subcommittee of the banking and commerce committee of that other place, consisting of Senators Hayden, Farris and Roebuck, each of whom is a very eminent counsel in his own right, studied the question. They made a large number of amendments; thus there was a great temptation, when it came before the House of Commons committee, to take the bill as having received careful consideration by those who had dealt with it before, and to exercise our own judgment concerning it scarcely at all.
That is diametrically opposite to the treatment which was given to it by the House of Commons committee. We heard a large number of delegations; we received a large number of briefs. These briefs were all carefully digested. Every substantial point that was raised in them was earmarked against the section of the bill to which it referred. As that section of the bill was called it was discussed in the light of the points which had been made in these briefs, whether or not anyone had appeared to make a personal presentation in support of his brief. The result has been, as the hon. member for Lake Centre has indicated on a previous occasion, that we have a bill which could be quite safely introduced at another session of parliament without the necessity of hearing further representations. And in relation to a task as large as this one is, it would be only by that method that we could ever get it through within the compass of a single parliamentary session.
With regard to the Combines Investigation Act, my hon. friend says he thinks that a committee should be set up to consider the terms of this act and the changes or amendments that might be made to it. I am sorry I cannot agree with my hon. friend. As he will recall, it is less than two years ago since we had a long debate in this house concerning the report of another highly competent commission, the MacQuarrie committee. That committee had discharged ably the very task that the hon. member is now recommending should be assigned again to a parliamentary committee or some other royal commission. The MacQuarrie committee conducted the first complete inquiry made into the Combines Investigation Act, and recommended the first complete overhaul which it has had since it was first passed in 1923. And while I would not suggest for a moment that we should go on for another period of more than a quarter of a century without having another thorough examination of this act, I do not think it is necessary
Supply-Justice
to do so within two years after the MacQuarrie report was implemented.
My hon. friend made reference to the wire and cable inquiry. As I think he himself indicated, this inquiry was conducted by Mr. Carl Goldenberg, Q.C., of Montreal. He was appointed a special commissioner, and my hon. friend rather insinuated in his remarks that perhaps some report concerning that matter had been made to me, and he wanted to know what the standing of the matter was. My information is that Mr. Goldenberg held the final hearing fairly recently, at which the parties concerned exercised their right to be heard, and they were heard in February last. Since that time Mr. Goldenberg has been engaged in the preparation of his report, which we hope to receive about September of this year, and which of course will be considered by Mr. MacDonald and passed on to the restrictive trade practices commission in due course, if that seems to be the proper thing to do. It will not be until after the restrictive trade practices commission has considered it that it will come, if it does come at that time, to the minister. There is one other point that my hon. friend made, and that is that he thought we should examine our own statute in the light of the practice in the United States.
No, I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend says no. I was not going to suggest that we should examine it in the light of practice in the United States with a view to borrowing what the United States had done, but to examine it in the light of United States legislation-as I understood my hon. friend- with a view to not borrowing the United States principle, as he announced it, of saying that mere bigness was an offence in itself.
I would point out to my hon. friend-and I am not suggesting he is of this view-but many people are, and quite erroneously so, of the view that in Canada we have copied the United States in some parts of our legislation.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am glad to see my hon. friend shaking his head in the negative, because he and I are in agreement on this point. He knows, I am sure-as we all do in the House of Commons-that it would have been impossible for us to have copied the United States; because our original legislation, forming part of the criminal law of the country at that time, was passed a year before the earliest United States federal legislation, and therefore obviously could not have been based upon the United States legislation.

Supply-Justice
Then he raised one other matter in connection with loss leaders, and he wanted me to report to the house as to what conclusions had been reached in that investigation. The investigation is by no means complete, and will not be complete for some considerable time. I would hope that very likely we would be able to report the results of that by the time of the next parliament; but at the present time we have no report. And there has been, I suggest, no indication upon the part of the members of the commission, or of myself, at any time, that the report to which the hon. member has referred would be available within this present time.

When did the investigation begin, with a view to ascertaining whether or not loss leaders could be defined? I understand that various groups and bodies were communicated with in order to ascertain what they might suggest as to the definition of a loss leader-and it all turned out to be a lost cause.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, I accept my hon. friend's epigram as to the investigation in respect of loss leaders turning out to be a lost cause. It is a little premature, though, because we have not yet completed the investigation. And if I understood his argument correctly, I thought he himself was indicating or, shall I say, despairing of its being anything other than a lost cause; because the whole tenor of his argument was to the effect that it was impossible to define a loss leader.
I will agree that the experience of the MacQuarrie committee, the witnesses who appeared before that committee, and the witness who appeared before the parliamentary committee which was considering amendments to the Combines Investigation Act based upon the recommendations of the MacQuarrie committee, all indicated that there was a very genuine and a very great difficulty in defining a loss leader.
And of course, if we are going to deal with a subject of that sort, one of the first essentials is that we should have an accurate knowledge of what it is we are dealing with. That is the first essential if we are to make any progress.
The hon. member has asked when the investigation began. It began in November of 1952, just about the time the legislation was coming before the house. And it has continued actively from that time until the present in the form of inquiries by the director seeking the views of trade organizations in the retail and wholesale distributing trades, certain associations in specific industrial groups, and general business associations such as the Canadian Manufacturers Association

and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, as well as certain groups consisting of departmental stores, co-operative associations, chain stores and the like, and consumer groups which would include farm and labour groups. The compilation of the views of all these various concerns, to say nothing of the reaching of conclusions based upon that compilation, is a heavy task, one which as yet has been by no means completed.
Did the minister mean that it was in November, 1951, that this investigation started?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: November, 1952.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The legislation was passed in June of 1952.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, yes; my hon. friend is quite right when he says that. I was asked the question as to when it started, and I am now giving the date upon which it did start.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: My only reason for the interjection was that the minister had said that it was at the time the legislation was coming before the house. The legislation had been passed in the previous session.
Mr. Chairman, I want to take this opportunity of raising a serious problem with which the municipalities in Manitoba are faced.

I wonder if my hon.
friend would permit the minister to complete his statement. There was one other question he did not answer, as to how many prosecutions had taken place since December, 1951, under the legislation covering retail price maintenance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, what I was going to suggest is this, in relation to the remarks of the hon. member for Lake Centre and the hon. member for Selkirk, that I believe we would make for more orderly progress in committee if we were to discuss the various items in this department as they are called, item by item. For instance, if my hon. friend from Selkirk is going to refer to penitentiaries-
No, I am not. I will later on, but not just now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Could we go through the estimates item by item? I would be very glad to discuss each one as it is called. I do suggest however that we would make better progress if we were to follow that procedure. Otherwise we will be jumping from one subject to another.

I think it is only fair that the hon. member for Selkirk should be per-

mitted to proceed, because I believe I interrupted him when I asked the minister for an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am quite agreeable that the hon. member for Selkirk should proceed. I am only suggesting that after we have disposed of the matters to which he refers we might begin the orderly process of considering each item separately.
There are one or two matters I wish to deal with before we consider the separate items.

Then, Mr. Chairman, I shall begin again. Let me take this opportunity, when the minister's estimates are before the house, to bring up a serious matter facing the municipalities in Manitoba in which there are airfields or military camps. Perhaps I would save the time of the committee if I were to quote an editorial from the Winnipeg Tribune of Thursday, May 7. Before I begin reading I should explain that I had asked for the correspondence that had passed between the town of Gimli and the Minister of Justice. The article states:
An interesting exchange of letters has taken place between the town of Gimli and Justice Minister Garson.
Last year several members of the R.C.A.F. stationed at Gimli were sentenced to prison. Their families applied to the town for relief. Gimli authorities did not feel that local taxpayers should be asked to pay the shot for this assistance. They contended that although the families had been there long enough to become "residents" under the letter of the law, they should not be regarded as permanent citizens.
The town of Gimli therefore wrote to Mr. Garson asking that the dominion government be financially responsible for the relief payments and that Ottawa acknowledge responsibility for those military dependents. In reply Mr. Garson has told Gimli that the federal government could not admit this responsibility and that the town would have to foot the relief bill. He said that Ottawa could not consider itself responsible for military dependents in the case any more than they could give help to dependents of civilian employees. He added that the town was benefited as a result of the R.C.A.F. station being nearby.
This last comment seems to be beside the point. But the case could be of interest not only to other municipalities near training centres and stations of the armed services but to the provincial government as well. It should be borne in mind that the Manitoba government has accepted a measure of responsibility for relief costs. The provincial government has agreed to pay 60 per cent of the cost of relief above a certain stipulated minimum. The rest is paid by the municipalities. The municipalities and the province have long contended that the dominion government should shoulder the relief burden. Ottawa authorities implicitly acknowledged that relief costs should be their responsibility in their offer to the provinces in 1945.
The reply to Mr. Garson should be of course that the federal government should be responsible for these military dependents and for civilian cases as
Supply-Justice
well. Provincial authorities should join with the town of Gimli in trying to convince Mr. Garson and his cabinet colleagues that relief costs should properly be borne by the dominion government.
Taking the correspondence that has been exchanged between the town of Gimli and the minister, I will not read all of the letter of the town of December 11, 1952, but I should like to point out that the town draws attention to this fact:
Recently several airmen from the Gimli airport were convicted by a police magistrate for various crimes involving the theft of goods from government stores and were sentenced to terms of imprisonment from five to nine months. We understand that further charges of a similar nature are being laid and also that some who have already been charged are awaiting trial in higher courts. In other words, there is the possibility of this growing and involving many men and probably some for comparatively long terms.
Our concern is chiefly for the wives and families of these men so convicted. Under existing legislation it would appear that, if they have lived here long enough to have gained residence, that they become wards of the town. As these men were in Her Majesty's service when convicted it would seem that there should be some dominion or provincial responsibility for those who were depending on them and are now left destitute by this action.
I do not need to read any more of that letter because that makes the point. But in the minister's reply of February 5, 1953, he drew the attention of the town of Gimli to the fact that he had received a letter from the Department of National Defence and went on to say:
That department has now indicated that it does not consider that the dependents of convicted service personnel are in a different position from that of the employees of a civilian firm who are brought into a community to work for their employer and to bring their dependents with them. Where the employees in question are sentenced to imprisonment the employer does not make special provision for the maintenance of the dependents.
Then there is this further paragraph:
The department points out that the location of an air force station or other military establishment of a considerable size such as that at Gimli results in substantial benefits to the community in question in the form of increased trade by local merchants, the fulfilling of housing requirements and the provision of other services. Service personnel and their dependents who reside in a community are generally accepted as ordinary citizens and the department considers that they should be treated as such under all circumstances.
What the minister does not take into consideration is that when an airfield, air training base or other military establishment is set up no taxes are paid. If a manufacturing concern moves into a town it pays taxes and the people who work for the manufacturer pay taxes. The people who work for the foundry or other manufacturing concern that is established in a town buy their goods and services in the town. People in the air force

Supply-Justice
or army can buy anything they want in the canteen cheaper than it can be bought in any town in Manitoba. Therefore I do not think it is a fair comparison for the minister to say that it is just like another business. It is not like another business at all. It is something entirely different. The minister went on to say in his letter:
The department points out, however, that under the present law, where military personnel are sentenced to imprisonment and are released from the force as a result thereof, which is usually the case, the dependents may be issued with second class transportation and the necessary meal tickets for the journey to the place in Canada indicated by the serviceman as being his place of residence at the time of enrolment in the force.
If they leave Gimli they may go to the minister's constituency of Marquette and become a burden on that municipality.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Then something will happen.
No, I do not say that. I do not want to labour the point, but the situation is not fair and it should be corrected.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If I may deal with these points as they are raised I think it may help. I deal with this present point with some embarrassment in that actually it is a matter which comes under other departments of government than my own. I think the reason for my having been written to in this connection was that I am the only minister from Manitoba. But if I might discuss this principle of fairness, which the hon. gentleman who is noted for his fairness has just enunciated, and venture quite modestly to disagree with him on the principle of fairness, I would put it in this way.
The editorial in the Winnipeg Tribune refers to the proposed green book settlement of 1945. It is true the dominion government of that day, as part of an over-all financial settlement between itself and the provincial governments represented at that conference, did indicate its willingness to take over what was then and is still now the responsibility of the provinces, namely, the payment of relief. It is also true that at that conference the province of Manitoba, which I had then the honour to represent, was the only province which, immediately the green book proposal was made, said Yes, we will accept this proposal. If all the provinces had accepted the proposal the point that my hon. friend is making today would not have arisen, and I think that the provinces as a whole would perhaps have been in a better position than they are at the present time. But they did not accept the proposal; they turned it down. After further negotiations a new proposal was made which took the form of the tax agreements which now exist between

the nine provinces of Canada and the dominion under which, so far as the province of Manitoba is concerned, in return for revenue sources which for that province at their peak produced $5-5 million, the province in this present year receives about $24 million in payments from the dominion treasury-upon the understanding that the provinces continue to be responsible for relief.
I am not suggesting that the difference between these two figures of $5-5 million and $24 million is an exact measure of the benefit to the Manitoba treasury of this tax agreement. But there is no doubt that the financial benefit to the Manitoba treasury is a very substantial one which has enabled the provincial government of Manitoba only recently to increase by $3-8 million the substantial benefits which it was already paying to Manitoba municipalities.
All of these arrangements were entered into in the light of the fact that in 1945 a proposal had been made to take over unemployment relief as a part of an over-all financial deal. It was rejected by the provinces and then these new tax agreements were entered into, which left the relief situation in the position in which it then stood and now stands. That being so-I know my hon. friend is fair-and I know of no fairer man in this house-how can he say that an arrangement which is enormously advantageous to the provinces in certain cases-and it is certainly so in the case of Manitoba-provides that the dominion government should assume the cost of relief, when it provides such thing.
My hon. friend says there is an inequity because when a military camp or an airport comes along taxes are not paid. Well, my hon. friend should know, because he was a member for that constituency at one time, that the airport at Gimli is not situated within the town of Gimli-it is the town of Gimli we are talking about-and no other municipality. He should also know that his other statement is wrong regarding these dependents of airmen who were convicted of offences, and that is the reason this whole question arises. When these dependents become tenants in the town of Gimli they pay taxes in their rent.
I am sure that my hon. friend knows enough of economics to know that in rent there is included the carrying charges of the taxes against the premises. It goes right to the landlord and from the landlord to the municipality. The whole question here is whether, in view of the present arrangements between the provinces and the federal

government-an arrangement into which they have freely entered-the burden of relief should in addition to and in spite of these arrangements be passed over to the federal government.
I am quite prepared to admit that from the standpoint of an over-all arrangement for the nation as a whole quite a good case can be made out for having relief handled in that way. But, when a number of governments have freely entered into an existing arrangement, while you may argue in the abstract that some other national arrangement is preferable, yet the governments concerned must conclude a bargain to that effect, and sign an agreement before they are bound. The fact of the matter is that the present agreements were signed only last year and, if I remember correctly, they have five years to run. If my hon. friend will permit me to say so, I do not think while those agreements are running it is fair for him to say that it is not fair for the dominion government to expect to carry on under an agreement which it has reached with the provinces-an agreement under which the province of my hon. friend and myself is receiving very large benefits.

I do not wish to debate the matter further because I have known the minister a very long time and I know enough not to get up against a lawyer when it comes to a debate. When you talk in a legal frame of mind you can make black look white.
I want to say, and I think the minister will still think I am fair, that I do not see it the way he sees it. In the tax agreement made with Manitoba in 1947 the federal government agreed to look after its own relief. Manitoba did not make any contract to take the discards of the army and the discards of the air force and feed them. That is what you are asking Gimli to do and that is what you are asking Macdonald to do, and other places. You throw them out and it does not matter whether you give them a railway ticket to go somewhere else or not, they are going to be dropped on somebody. You or the Minister of National Defence have taken the best out of them and do not want them any more. You should not ask the municipalities, which are hard up enough, to pay that money out.
I have said all that I am going to say but I do not think it is fair. The Department of National Defence should look after them and get them rehabilitated somewhere and not leave them in Gimli. Gimli has even had to pay hospital bills and so on for them. These people are there because the services put them there and there is no other reason.
Supply-Justice
They are not there because they wanted to live in Gimli.

Mr. Chairman, I rise at this moment on the first item of the minister's estimates to bring to his attention something which he might first regard as something of a trivial nature. The people who may be affected of course would not consider it to be trivial. I might say that I have been asked by the member for Battle River to bring the matter to the minister's attention because the hon member for Battle River is unable to be in the chamber at the present time. We are expecting to prorogue soon and members are trying to wind up other business.
I am going to speak in respect of measures that might be taken towards prosecutions for what might be termed very unfair business practices. I will give the minister an example of what I mean and he will be perhaps then more readily and properly able to answer the question. I have in my hand an article which happens to be a belt that a man uses to hold up his trousers.
It is a good idea.

When the belt breaks the result is liable to be catastrophic. The purchaser of this belt went into a store one day-and it happened to be in the constituency of Battle River although I suppose the same thing might have happened in almost any constituency-and he picked up a belt and noticed on the label on the package the words "genuine cowhide". He took the belt, looked at it and found stamped inside the belt "genuine cowhide". He thought, "Well, that is pretty good," and he bought the belt. I do not know whether it happened the first time he buckled the belt up but anyway the belt broke. On examining the belt he found it was not cowhide at all and that it was just nothing but paper. He had bought a paper belt. Now, I am going to send this over to the minister. He had better not wear it or he may know something about an embarrassing moment. I am going to send it over to him, and he can read on the label "genuine cowhide", and he can read the lettering stamped on the belt "genuine cowhide". He can see the place where the belt broke, and it is nothing but paper.
I may tell him the rest of the story. The gentleman who bought this belt went back to his dealer and said, "Here, I thought this was a genuine cowhide belt; it says so on the package and it says so on the belt." The manager of the store looked at it and said, "That is bad." He looked at the rest of his stock and found that they were the same type of belt, so he sent the whole shipment back to the wholesaler, which of course was the

Supply-Justice
proper thing to do. All we wish to say is the manufacturer had no right to sell goods misrepresented such as that is, and in our opinion a manufacturer who does that should be prosecuted. I should like the minister to answer two questions. First, what is the position of the manufacturer and the wholesaler in a case of this kind? Secondly, what procedure should an individual take? I see the minister is burning the end of the belt.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is paper, all right.

If the minister can light it, and it flares up like that, it must be paper. You cannot light solid leather with a match. What is the position of the manufacturer and wholesaler in a case like that? What is the procedure that should be taken when an individual buys a product like that? The individual might take it back to the store and the storekeeper might even give him another and genuine belt, but that would not settle the matter. Another belt would hold up his trousers, but there is still the misrepresentation. It is a matter of dishonesty.
We might conclude that the odd belt was wrongly stamped, and that might be a good excuse. But the storekeeper looked at the shipment and found they were all the same, so he sent them back. That is a different matter.
A man never knows when he is safe these days.
As my hon. friend says, a man never knows when he is safe with just paper around his waist. I should like the minister to answer that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I imagine there is a federal statute, the Criminal Code or the Weights and Measures Act or some such statute as that which requires that one who puts out a product of this sort, being stamped and purporting to be a certain product, is responsible if it falls short of the representation which was placed upon it. Whether or not that would cover a paper belt, stamped as "genuine cowhide", I should not like to say offhand without consulting the statute. I will say this, Mr. Chairman: if it does not cover it, it certainly should. I shall check to see whether or not it is. If it is not covered, we should certainly introduce an amendment to the proper act in short order. We want to keep up the trousers of the nation.

I recognize that the minister realizes the principle involved, but is the wholesaler or manufacturer liable to prosecution? That is the thing I should like to know. If so, what procedure must be taken? Must a chap run off to a policeman and report to him?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The simple answer to the hon. member's question would be for him to consult the crown prosecutor in his district. My only reason for qualifying my reply to the hon. member's question is that it is very difficult for one who has been presented with a torn paper belt to say that this comes under section so and so of an act, without even looking at the act. There are federal statutes which are passed for the express purpose of prohibiting this sort of thing generally. In order to successfully prosecute an accused in a case of this kind, one must bring his case under some section of an existing statute.
If there is a lacuna in that statute, if there is a gap, and they have not thought of this particular matter, it may be that it is not covered by an existing law. As I said before, if it is not covered it certainly should be and I shall be glad, over the dinner recess, to make a check to see whether or not this product is covered.

We are in the process of trying to get through the estimates and so forth, so I wonder if this would be satisfactory to the minister? Will he pass this over to one of his officials and drop a line to the hon. member for Battle River? Would he mind doing that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I shall be glad to do that.
The minister might let me have the belt back.

There are two questions which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister and this house on the first item. The first has to do with the price war in cigarettes which has been under way in Vancouver-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Might I interrupt for a
moment? I wonder if we might start going through the estimates, and then deal with these matters as they come up? The point to which my hon. friend is referring now comes under the heading of the Combines Investigation Act, and I shall be glad to deal with it.

Unfortunately, it does not come under the Combines Investigation Act as that act reads now. I would prefer to place these two questions before the minister on this item. In Vancouver, for nearly two months, there has been a price war in cigarettes. In my opinion the chain stores have been using them as a loss leader. The business of these chain stores is primarily that of selling food and not cigarettes. The result of this price war has been to upset greatly the small stores which rely on cigarette sales for their main business.

I have some advertisements here from the Vancouver papers showing that the chain stores have been selling one package of 20 cigarettes for 31 cents, 3 packages for 89 cents and 10 packages for $2.95. Until recently it was costing the small tobacco store proprietor $2.91 for ten packages. Hence, if he was to compete with the chain store he had a margin of only four cents on ten packages. I believe that the distributors have now lowered the price to the small merchant to some extent and that he has a margin of 30 cents on ten packages.
I am sure the minister will agree that the little fellow simply cannot compete with these prices which are being charged by the chain stores. The small merchant depends on his tobacco business for his livelihood. I am told that in Vancouver there are over 2,000 people who are affected, many of whom are veterans and others who are handicapped in one way or another. There is a great deal of concern about the matter. These small merchants are convinced that they are just being run out of business by the chain stores. I submit that the small merchant in any community is the backbone of our merchandising system. It is not right that he should be subjected to unfair competition of this kind.
During the second session of 1951 this question was considered by a special committee to which some reference was made earlier in the afternoon. In their report which was made on December 7, 1951, I find this paragraph:
Certain groups appearing before the committee have expressed the view that one of the consequences of prohibiting resale price maintenance will be to enable large and powerful retailing interests to engage in a policy of selling goods at unreasonably low prices for the purpose of destroying the independent retailer.
My opinion is that that is what is being done in the cigarette war in Vancouver. The report continues:
This committee does not think that under present conditions there is any substantial likelihood of such policies being engaged in but would recommend to the government, in the event of such policies being practised, the vigorous enforcement of section 498A of the Criminal Code which reads as follows . . .
Then the committee report sets out section 498A. There we have from a special committee of the house a clear-cut recommendation as to what action should be taken by the minister in the event of there arising a situation such as that which exists in Vancouver today. There is a further and final paragraph of the report which reads as follows:
Your committee is of the view that if other types of predatory price cutting, the possibility and the nature of which cannot at the present time be
Supply-Justice
foreseen, take place, the government should then consider placing before parliament further amendments of the Combines Investigation Act or the Criminal Code prohibiting such other types of predatory price cutting and providing adequate penalties for them.
There again we have a definite recommendation of a course of action to be followed by the government in the event of there being this predatory price cutting.
The minister has spoken of investigations. Apparently there have been bodies investigating for some time. As a matter of fact, in the annual report of the director of investigation and research for the year ended March 31, 1953, there is at page 27 a reference to one of those investigations. But unfortunately, investigating the matter is not going to help the small merchant out in Vancouver. He may very well be bankrupt long before any report has been filed by the people who are making this investigation.
I would ask the minister to tell us today what action, if any, is going to be taken by his department. When the minister mentioned these investigations a few moments ago he said-if I understood him correctly-that he did not expect a report for many months yet. I should like to know why the first recommendation of the special committee cannot be followed. That recommendation was that section 498A of the Criminal Code could be used to meet a situation of this kind. I would also ask the minister why it has not been possible during the present session to bring in some legislation such as that recommended in the final paragraph of the report of the committee.
I believe that these small merchants must not be forced to the wall. If the chain stores are allowed to get away with this action on cigarettes, it is only a question of time until they will be taking steps which will affect some other group of small merchants. In view of the stand the minister took in 1951 during the discussion of this whole question of resale price maintenance, I think he is morally bound to take action now that there have actually come to pass the things which we warned him would happen. I believe there is an obligation on him and on the government to take some action to meet this situation.
The other question I wish to place before the minister concerns the province of British Columbia as well. It concerns the district in which I was born and in which I still have family connections, namely the Kootenay district in southeastern British Columbia. It is this Doukhobor question. Ten days ago or two weeks ago the minister had talks

Supply-Justice
here with the attorney general of British Columbia concerning this question. This is only one of many talks that have taken place between a Minister of Justice of Canada and an attorney general of British Columbia on the Doukhobor question down through the years. The minister has not made a report to the house on the result of these conversations but I wish to emphasize to him the importance of the dominion government giving to the people of British Columbia justification for believing that the federal government is prepared to do its share toward bringing about a settlement of this problem. There is now a feeling that the dominion has been brushing aside the representations of the province.
I have here an editorial from the Vancouver Sun which is one of the strong supporters of this government. It was written shortly before the attorney general of British Columbia came to Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in order to save my hon. friend the need for developing an argument of this sort, may I say that I had this talk with Mr. Bonner-

If I may, I should just like to finish my statement. Then the minister can make his answer. I do not want to be cut off in the middle of my submission.
This is the leading editorial of the day and it is entitled, "Bon Voyage to Bonner". The first paragraph reads as follows:
B.C. will wish Attorney-General Bonner miraculous luck-
And I stress that word "miraculous".
B.C. will wish Attorney General Bonner miraculous luck in his demand for federal aid and money to get the sons of freedom "removed immediately from this province."
The minister knows that the sons of freedom is the portion or sect of the Doukhobor settlement which is causing all the trouble. The editorial continues:
He'll need it to crack Ottawa's unvarying thirty-year refusal to shoulder any real responsibility for the terror and trouble freedomite fanatics have inflicted on B.C.
Previous provincial governments have ardently shared Mr. Bonner's wish. They've begged and pleaded with Ottawa to recognize that, in bringing the Doukhobors to Canada, the federal government assumed a responsibility for their subsequent outrages which it can't morally shove onto B.C.
But Ottawa has always straight-armed such appeals. Federal authorities smugly dismissed B.C.'s trouble as "a question of law enforcement for which the provincial government is responsible."
And I think I heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the Minister of Justice

use these words in the house the other day. The editorial goes on:
At most Ottawa would dispatch some extra mounties to the Kootenays when mass outbreaks threatened.
That editorial accurately summarizes the attitude which has been taken by successive dominion governments on this Doukhobor problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not agree with that for a moment.

Here we have a situation in British Columbia where in one of these districts, according to press dispatches of May 4:
More than twenty homes, as well as a community hall, an unoccupied store and a sawmill, have been put to the torch in the last month.
Railway tracks have also been bombed.
Residents have started armed night patrols to guard their homes and businesses against further violence.
The spiritual leader of the sons of freedom sect, who is down in South America looking for a new home for them, said, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of May 11:
The spiritual leader of the sons of freedom, speaking from a foreign land, has said he won't use his influence with his unruly flock unless the federal government will help him solve the Doukhobor problem "once and for all".
"The Doukhobors are not my problem", said Stefan Sorokin. "They are Canadians and the Canadian government should be concerned over them."
The dispatch went on in another paragraph to say this:
The long-absent Sorokin, in Uruguay looking for a new home for his people, says he won't return to try to smooth things over in the Kootenays unless he can get help from the federal government.
I suggest to the minister that there are at least two things that could be done. I admit that the problem is dreadfully difficult. I do not know that these are the answers to the question, but I do make two suggestions. In the first place, the dominion government should say to the provincial government that one-half of the costs occasioned by this trouble will be met by the dominion government. The province of British Columbia is to be faced with an expenditure of about $300,000 this year, and perhaps more, if this trouble continues; that money is to be used for special guards on railways, bridges and school houses, and other special measures which have to be taken to meet the situation. In view of the background of this situation, it is only fair that the two governments should team up and make a joint approach to a settlement.
The second situation is this. Why is it not possible for the Department of External Affairs to co-operate with this spiritual leader and with anyone else who is trying

to find a home for this sect in another country? The representatives of the sect went to Costa Rica. We were told there was a reasonable chance of their migrating to that country. Now he is in Uruguay, and there might be a chance of their moving there. I should think it would be possible for the government, through the Department of External Affairs, to give considerable help in arranging for a migration of that type. If that can be done, this whole problem will be settled.
Unfortunately, this particular sect seems to be completely unwilling to adopt the laws of Canada and settle down as ordinary citizens. They have been carrying on in this way for many years; in fact ever since I was a small boy, and I do not see any prospect of settling the problem in the near future unless a far greater effort is made than there has been up to the present time. I should be very grateful if the minister could deal with these two questions.

As the member representing the constituency in which the great majority of the Doukhobors and the sons of freedom reside, I wish to take this opportunity to make a few remarks on this question. My constituents have been very concerned about this problem for quite a number of years, and recent events, house burnings, railroad bombings and that kind of thing, have increased that concern and indignation and have about completely exhausted their patience. However, to save the time of the committee, I think I can place before hon. members the attitude of the people at this time by reading briefly from an editorial of the Nelson Daily News as follows:
Need greater police strength to control sabotage In Kootenay.
Continuing attacks against power lines smack of a purpose more serious than religious zealots protesting against a way of life with which they do not fully agree.
The Kootenay-Boundary over the years has become almost used to fires that destroy homes of sons of freedom sect members, schools and barns. These are serious enough, but something more deadly has shown itself in more recent incidents. The week-end dynamiting of power lines feeding from West Kootenay to East Kootenay, and recent burning and bombing of bridges and destruction of sawmills are attacks against men's lives and livelihood. They must be regarded as something more serious than the usual outbreaks that are laid at the sons of freedom's door. These attacks equal the viciousness of those that plagued the railways and power companies in the thirties: they exceed in seriousness, if not in number, the outbreaks of 1947 and 1949-50.
The Kootenay has shown an admirable tolerance and a willingness to uphold the latest efforts in the sons of freedom problem; citizens are entitled to expect, however, adequate protection while these efforts are being carried forward as we should be
Supply

Justice
able to expect them to be when the government gets around to acting on the recommendations arising from the latest studies.
The government referred to in the editorial is the provincial government of British Columbia. As I said before, Mr. Chairman, patience in my constituency is about exhausted. In this connection, there have been many meetings, and some suggest to the authorities they may have to take the matter into their own hands. I have had some personal experience with this problem, since I know personally a large number of Doukhobors. I want to make quite clear the distinction between the 10,000 law-abiding persons known as Doukhobors and the 2,500 persons known as sons of freedom. The sons of freedom belong to a small sect whose burnings and bombings are supposed to be exhibitions of protest against the Canadianiza-tion of the majority of the Doukhobor community.
On a good many occasions since coming to Ottawa I have had the opportunity to discuss this matter with the Minister of Justice. I have found him most anxious to secure information and to hear suggestions. I must say I have found him most co-operative in listening to representations and opinions. I have found that the minister has a great deal of sympathy for any government in British Columbia, regardless of political stripe, that has to face this longstanding and most difficult and complicated question. Without a doubt, it is the outstanding, serious social problem created by any one group in Canada at this time. Furthermore I have found the minister has a great deal of sympathy for the people of the Kootenays and the surrounding country who, in the light of their experiences throughout the years, have now almost exhausted their patience.
I find also that the minister is most anxious to do all he can to support any provincial government that puts into writing satisfactory proposals and on which can be based a satisfactory policy. I might say in that connection that, to date, there has not been a single government in British Columbia that has accepted its full responsibilities in this matter, and has outlined to the federal government-any federal	government-a
written policy or proposal to deal with this matter in a co-operative way.
Owing to the urgent demands of the people in Kootenay West, who are seriously affected, the attorney general of British Columbia came to Ottawa early in May and discussed this situation with the Minister of Justice.

Supply-Justice
Then shortly afterwards the premier of the province who had been speaking at Trail, on the insistence of a group of people who are very concerned with this situation, sent a wire to the Prime Minister of Canada urging certain action. I shall deal with that wire first of all. According to the statement by the Minister of Justice the wire was in these words:
Doukhobor situation in Kootenays extremely critical. Unless some action taken immediately expect violence will break out. Strongly recommend that your government under the powers of the War Measures Act proclaim an immediate curfew on all Doukhobors in the Kootenay district of British Columbia.
When I heard the minister read that telegram, when replying to my question a few days ago, I was simply horrified to think that any provincial premier in Canada at this time would suggest that the War Measures Act be invoked, thus giving the government of Canada unlimited authority over all property and civil rights and of persons in peacetime. Such action would make it possible for the federal government to freeze wages, direct people to employment, and to do many other things required in wartime. I am sure when the premier of British Columbia sent that telegram he was not fully aware of the implications of giving effect to the War Measures Act.
Second, I was greatly surprised to see that the premier suggested that there should be a curfew in respect of all Doukhobors in British Columbia. That confusion is possible because of the attitude of many people in that province who continuously confuse the Doukhobors with the sons of freedom. This outlook arises because of elections act legislation. For instance, in British Columbia a Doukhobor is any person who, under the elections act, is the descendant of a Doukhobor, and for that reason cannot vote.
There are bachelors of science, bachelors of art, presidents of chambers of commerce, active workers in trade unions and businessmen generally who at the present time are denied the vote. What surprised me was to have the premier of British Columbia suggesting that this government give effect to the War Measures Act and establish a curfew on all Doukhobors in British Columbia. In sending that telegram he must have failed to realize that if this government had acceded to his wishes it would have meant a gross indignity to the wife of one of his own cabinet ministers by prohibiting her from going out after sunset.
I mention these facts because I am sure the premier did not realize the full implications of his telegram. May I say, as one who

has always defended the Doukhobors who are good citizens, many of whom are becoming incorporated in our Canadian life, and have advocated that they be given the franchise, that we in this group will severally protest against the use of any curfew by any government that would limit the freedom of such fine persons as I have described.
I might say that the present pernicious election law on the statute books of British Columbia, placed there by a Conservative government, has prevented thousands of good citizens from exercising their franchise. It is that type of legislation and attitude which to some extent has fed the fires of discontent in this splinter group known as the sons of freedom.
And now I should like to make a few remarks about the government's reply. I have studied this question closely, and I have personal knowledge of it. I have employed some of these people and have met and known hundreds of them. I think the government's reply was made on sound grounds. The Acting Prime Minister was correct when he suggested that it is a constitutional responsibility of the provincial government to administer law and justice in the province. On that account this government has asked the government of British Columbia to submit in writing its policy to meet this situation. When that policy is submitted in writing, and if it is mutually satisfactory to both governments, my understanding is that this government is willing to give its support to such a policy.
The telegram in reply indicates in every way a willingness on the part of the government to co-operate with, and to support and co-operate with the provincial government in British Columbia, in dealing with this unfortunate situation. Upon asking a question of the minister this morning I was very much surprised to learn that, although early in May the attorney general of British Columbia was in Ottawa discussing this question with the Minister of Justice, and although he knows the urgent nature and the seriousness of the situation, the concern of the railroaders, those who are operating the trains, and the views of the people in the Slocan and other valleys in which these sons of freedom live, so many days have passed without this government having received proposals from the government of British Columbia, or any notification in writing as to its policy.
I could speak at some considerable length on this subject, but I shall not further trespass on the time of the house. I must bring to the attention of the minister, as I have done before-and I know it is fully recognized by him-that this is a most peculiar

and serious problem in my constituency. I do urge that just as soon as he receives the written policy from the government of British Columbia he should place those proposals before the cabinet, with a view to bringing about an agreement concerning policy and action. Just as soon as possible this government should do all it can to assist the government of British Columbia in maintaining law and order, and by making a financial contribution toward the cost of solving this problem in a satisfactory manner.
The problem has both immediate and longterm aspects. I do not include in that one small group of trouble makers even all the sons of freedom. Some of these people in my opinion are infants led by a small group of lunatics; and it is that small group of lunatics with which the governments of British Columbia and of Canada must deal sternly if they are to stop these serious violations of the law in the Kootenay district.
That is the immediate problem. The next problem is that of long-term measures to win these people away from the small group which has control and to incorporate the Doukhobor community as a whole in our general Canadian community. Another step in that connection is to do all we can to bring to bear upon the government of British Columbia the necessity for an amendment to the elections act which at the present time denies the franchise to thousands of good Canadians. The act should be amended to give these people the opportunity to exercise their franchise and in that way to become fully incorporated into our Canadian community.

I want to bring a matter to the minister's attention which I think shows a rather distressing disregard by people in his department for the problems of individuals. I want to read a letter written to me recently by a lawyer in Toronto, Mr. W. R. Allen of the firm of Allen and Meyrick. I will be glad to give the letter to the minister. I will not mention the lawyer's client by name because he has requested me not to do so, but it is in the letter and the minister can see it there. I think he will realize the reasons for not mentioning the client's name. In the letter he says:
I acted for one . . . who was convicted on September 19, 1952, at Lindsay, Ontario, of uttering a forged cheque. He was sentenced to eight months in the reformatory and served his time at Rideau industrial farm, Burritts Rapids. In December application was made on his behalf for a remission of sentence based on the following facts:
1.	He spent two months approximately in custody awaiting trial, most of which was at the request of the crown attorney in order to complete and further their investigation.
2.	His wife was living in Vancouver with him and their child at the time of his arrest and being
Supply-Justice
unable to provide for her own living, she was returned to Toronto, and I am informed that she was forced to accept relief intermittently.
3.	. . . was hospitalized at the industrial farm for a conviction which led to his discharge from the army one year previous.
4.	. . . was the recipient of a citation order for gallantry during the second world war.
5.	A former employer guaranteed employment upon his release.
On January 23, 1953, I brought all of these facts to the attention of Mr. A. A. Moffat, remission branch, Department of Justice, Ottawa, who advised me on January 31, 1953, that the case was already under investigation. On April 17, 1953, I was advised by Ph. Thibault for undersecretary of state that "the Solicitor General of Canada has found himself unable to advise His Excellency the Governor General to interfere with the sentence imposed by the court."
Then Mr. Allen goes on to say:
On the day previous to the date of this letter, April 15, 1953, . . . telephoned me to say that he had been released from the industrial farm and had already returned to work. You will appreciate the embarrassment that this situation could cause a solicitor to be advised by the Department of the Secretary of State that a man had been refused remission after he had been released. Our profession treats the matter of remissions very seriously, particularly in a case of this type where it is a wife and child who are suffering hardships, and I would not like to think that there is any unnecessary delay in the processing of these applications by the department.
X bring this to the minister's attention because I think it shows where bureaucracy can lead us. This lawyer is a very reasonable and sensible man, and he put forward what I think is a reasonable and sensible case. He brought the case to the attention of the government. His application lay around for two and a half months. It seems obvious that the Solicitor General then had it brought to his attention and said to himself: oh well, we had better do something about this matter because it has been around for quite a while. He then wrote a routine letter, as so often seems to be the case when we apply on behalf of individuals, saying in very pious terms that nothing could be done.
Then it turned out, as is so often the case, that the lance-corporal in the orderly room was a much more reasonable and sensible sort of person than the people higher up. It always seemed to be that way in the army. He took the matter into his own hands, followed the reasonable course and released the man before his sentence had expired.
I think this shows how a ridiculous situation can develop. The man was released the day before the Solicitor General wrote a pious letter saying that the case had been thoroughly investigated and that the government could not see its way clear to apply to the Governor General for clemency. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister because I hope that he will see to it that his colleague, the Solicitor General, and the other people in his

Supply-Justice
department take these matters a little more seriously, and when they are brought to his attention I hope he will see that something of a reasonable nature is done.
Obviously a good case for early release was put forward on behalf of this man, and early release was accomplished, but so far as the Solicitor General was concerned-the second senior man in the justice department, as I understand it-the man could stay there and serve out his term. He completely washed his hands of it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Who is the Solicitor General now?
That is not good enough.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does the material in my hon. friend's possession disclose whether the prisoner was released after he had served his time or was he let out on remission?
He was let out on remission. I shall be very glad to give the minister the letter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In fairness to the very good staff that we have in the remissions branch I want to say that we handle about 10,000 applications for remission per annum, and that this is the first time in my four years' experience in the department when an error of this sort has occurred. During that time we have handled about 40,000 such cases, and I am sure that my hon. friend, being a businessman, would like to give his staff the benefit of not disapproving of them too much if they made a mistake in one case out of 40,000.
You cannot make mistakes with human beings.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend is under quite a misapprehension when he says that the Solicitor General simply sits there, looks at a letter and says to himself: what do I think about this, shall we let him out or not? That is not what happens at all. When an application for remission is made it goes into the department. A file is opened for it. Then a letter is written to the magistrate or judge who convicted the prisoner to obtain his opinion as to whether remission should be granted. The warden of the jail or penitentiary is also written to and a police report is obtained. In each case it is upon the basis of all these reports that the remission officers make a recommendation, and that recommendation having come to the Solicitor General or the Attorney General, as the case may be, it is acted upon by his attaching his signature to it.
I would be very glad to look into this matter to see what is the explanation of it,

but it could quite likely be simply a clerical mistake. My hon. friend, like some of the other statesmen of his party, makes his political appeals by making a great commotion when some clerk in the government service makes some minor error of procedure.
I am not complaining about some clerk in the government service. I am complaining that the Solicitor General did not pay any attention to the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend has no idea whatsoever as to what attention the Solicitor General paid to the matter because if it came before the Solicitor General and he rejected it he would do so upon recommendation of the officers of that department based upon a report from the judge or magistrate plus a report from the warden plus a report from the police. In no case is that judgment exercised until this material is considered, but it may very well have been that somewhere along the line of communication between the remission branch of the Department of Justice and the Department of the Secretary of State there has been a clerical error in connection with the communications to the legal firm and others concerned. If my hon. friend thinks that as a member of this House of Commons it is important enough for him to occupy his time and the time of us all, and make a great commotion-
Certainly it is his privilege. He should do it; it is his obligation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -I shall be very glad to look into it and tell my hon. friend exactly how the error arose. Doubtless it was an error, but it is not an error of any casual inattention on the part of the minister. It does not gel to the minister until it has gone through all of the stages I have mentioned.

I think we have had a very interesting statement by the minister. He finds it extraordinary that a member of parliament should stand up and take the time of the house to bring to the attention of the minister what he seriously considers to be an injustice to a Canadian citizen. I want to assure the minister that any time I think an injustice has been done to any single Canadian citizen I will take time, and all the time that I think I need in the house on it; and I believe that every other member of parliament will do the same thing.
We have certainly listened to a great explanation on behalf of the minister right now. The words that he used were that he did not think that a member of parliament should dare to bring-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.
You virtually said "dare".

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of privilege.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
You sit down.
I have as much right to the floor as you have.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. When the chairman is on his feet both hon. members must resume their seats.
The minister is rising on a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend has been quite unintentionally misrepresenting the point of view I endeavoured to express. I was endeavouring to express that in a matter of this kind the position could very easily have been resolved if my hon. friend had used the telephone. Inside of about thirty seconds we could have told him what the situation was. Then, if he thought there was anything that deserved the attention of the House of Commons, he could have come into this chamber and raised all the commotion he liked. I think he must give the government credit for a modicum of ordinary common sense. He might have known that where there is a report apparently put out by the Solicitor General and another put out by the Secretary of State, which are inconsistent, in all likelihood there has been some clerical mix-up along the line and that it is quite explicable.
I have no objection to the commotion. I want to make it perfectly clear that this is a matter for every member to decide for himself; that is, whether he desires to make a commotion about something of this sort in the House of Commons. That is his right and privilege and I would be the last man to take any objection to it; but I have been in the habit in matters of this kind of settling the affair by way of a telephone call.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You have never been in opposition.

Are we to deal with everything by the telephone? Is it not the right of a member sent here by his constituents to bring up a matter on the floor of the house? That should be his privilege, and he does not have to use the telephone. If my friend believes that this is the place to bring the matter up he should not be instructed by the minister to hush it up by using the telephone. This is a matter which
Supply-Justice
has been exposed today on the floor of the House of Commons indicating carelessness on the part of some person in the minister's department-gross carelessness.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Can we not pass on to the next item?
After all, it was just a human being incarcerated in jail.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Can we not pass on to the next item, which is the remission item?

Mr. Chairman, I think this is the proper place to draw to the minister's attention what seems to be a very serious situation in connection with smuggling, particularly smuggling of cigarettes. I have here the report of the R.C.M.P. for the year ending March 31, 1952. On page 17 I read that in the year 1951-52 there were 67,000-odd seizures of smuggled cigarettes. I read further on that the quantity seized, again speaking of cigarettes, is approximately 400 per cent greater than in the preceding year. I find also that in the year ending March 31, 1953, seizures again apparently almost doubled and there were 115,415 seizures. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to take up too much time. I could speak at great length upon this subject, because it is quite a large one. The situation is this. These facts to which my hon. friend has referred were reported to us and it was suggested in the first instance that the cigarette manufacturers had been guilty of an offence under section 498A of the Criminal Code in that they were allegedly giving to the chains a more favourable discount than they were making available to, shall I say, the orthodox wholesalers.
We have investigated that charge and, upon the basis of the data which we have so far received, have discovered that it is without foundation; that is to say, we have found that the chains buy from the manufacturers on the same basis for like quantities -the quality being the same in the case of cigarettes-as do the wholesalers, and that the lower price at which the chains sell to their customers is the product of two factors: one, that the chain wholesale subsidiary or wholesale associate takes a lower wholesale mark-up and that the chains themselves take a lower retail mark-up than does the ordinary wholesaler on the one hand or the ordinary retailer on the other hand.
But neither of these two acts-that is, the taking of a lower mark-up in the wholesale line or a lower mark-up in the retail line- is an offence under the law. Certainly from the standpoint of the consumer, I am sure that he would greatly question whether it should ever be made an offence because, for the first time in a long history of cigarette and tobacco selling, we have at the present time a competitive condition which has brought about a substantial reduction in price to the consumer.

It will be found by my hon. friend, if he wishes to investigate the matter, that while the mark-up that has been taken by the chain stores is, as I have indicated, lower than it previously had been when resale price maintenance was permitted, the mark-up which is taken on cigarettes does not vary greatly from what the chains take on many other item of merchandise. Hence if we are going to say that we should create an offence and say that it is contrary to law for a free enterpriser-a wholesaler or a retailer-in this country to carry out his function in relation to distribution for a low charge, then we would have to apply that same principle right across the board to coffee, soap, cheese and everything that is sold in that way.
I greatly doubt that the Canadian people would be in favour of following that practice. Where you have a situation such as that which exists today, where in many lines of merchandise it takes as much money to get the product from the manufacturer's door to the consumer as it does to manufacture it, I think there will be quite a strong view, especially among consumers, that it is rather a good thing when the costs of distribution can be reduced.

I wish to point out to the minister that there is a grave housing shortage in Kingston. This procedure was all right when the farmers had plenty of outlets for their cheese, butter, milk and so on, but there is no shortage of milk around that district at the present time. The land creates a bottleneck in the plans of Kingston city to provide services for the districts which lie beyond this land.
As the minister knows, there are over 700 acres of land there. The greater part of this land is used only for pasture. Hay has been cut off it for several years and stacked. I remember several years when the hay would

be sold, probably during the fall or the next spring, and would bring about $1 a ton, a price which did not even pay for the gasoline or the feed for the horses while it was being cut.
